newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers meet to finalise details on EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers meet to finalise details on EMU.

text.p: EU finance ministers, confident that their plans for economic and monetary union will remain firmly on track, met on Saturday to finalise important details for the single currency's 1999 launch date.

Heartened by news that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl will stand for re-election next year, the ministers, accompanied by central bankers from the 15-nation bloc, are expected to clarify the timetable for deciding which countries will join EMU.
The preferred time horizon appears to be late-April 1998, a period seen particularly helpful to France which holds parliamentary elections in March next year.
"It's a very reasonable forecast," Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, forerunner to a European Central Bank, told reporters.

After weeks of intense speculation that the 1999 start date might have to be delayed, Kohl's announcement, coupled with recent upbeat German economic figures, should give the group a chance to reaffirm a timely launch for EMU.
"I think the most important function of this meeting is to confirm once again that this process is on track," Swedish central bank governor Urban Backstrom told reporters.

Uncertainty over Bonn's ability to put its public finances in order in 1997, the critical year for those wishing to join the single currency club, have been primarily behind renewed market speculation that a postponement might be needed.
Difficulties on the budget front have been compounded by record unemployment in Germany and a political backdrop of widening labour unrest and public hostility to a common currency.
But Kohl's decision to stand again gave nearly all the ministers and central bankers renewed confidence in their assessment of the future.
"It is an important decision in favour of the realisation of EMU," Italian Finance Minister Carlo Azaglio Ciampi told reporters during a meeting in this Dutch resort town.
But Luxembourg's Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker told reporters he was never in any doubt about Europe's political commitment towards monetary union.
"It doesn't come as a great relief for me because I never had these doubts," Juncker said.

Apart from agreeing a time-frame for deciding the single currency's initial members, the group will also scrutinise a few remaining details of the Stability and Growth Pact, an accord designed to enforce budgetary discipline.
"We will discuss the stability pact and its detailed formulation. That's the theme today," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters.
The pact, agreed in principle by EU leaders in Dublin last December, seeks to penalise governments within monetary union which run annual deficits above three percent of GDP.
The maximum penalty under the accord is 0.5 percent of total output, and today's task is to determine whether such fines should be cumulative in nature.
